title: Speaking practice: Pictures, Stories, and Choices
description: Eight speaking tasks. Students describe a market scene, test an umbrella material, make up a story, explain a hallway rule, retell a short story, add fractions, share library information, and choose between two ways to vote. Students record two takes; teachers or students review the recordings.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Read about an outdoor market on a sunny day.

In the front, a woman in a green apron sells oranges and bananas from a wooden table. Behind her, a man holds a red balloon. Two children stand near a blue umbrella and look at a toy kite. A brown dog sleeps under the table. In the background, there are three tall trees.
Your friend has not been to the market. Describe the scene in your own words so your friend can imagine it.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A class tested three materials to find the best one for a rain umbrella. They held each material over a cup and poured water on top. Here are the results.
Paper towel: the water went through, and the cup was wet.
Cotton cloth: some water went through, and the cup was damp.
Plastic sheet: no water went through, and the cup stayed dry.
Tell your class which material you choose for the umbrella.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Imagine this scene from a story. Kofi stands at the edge of a swimming pool with his goggles on. His toes grip the edge. His arms are crossed, and he looks down at the water. His swim teacher, Ms. Lin, stands in the water and holds out her hand. Behind Kofi, two classmates cheer.
Make up what happens next. Tell your story to the class with a beginning, a middle, and an end.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A family has just moved to your town. They ask you about the public library. Use this fact card to tell them about it.
Open: Monday to Saturday, 9:00 to 6:00. Closed on Sunday.
Library card: free for anyone who lives in town.
Borrowing: up to 10 books for three weeks.
Story time for young children: Tuesdays at 4:00.
Also: 20 computers and a quiet room on the second floor.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: You are a fifth-grade buddy for a first-grade student named Omar. Omar asks you, “Why do we have to walk in the hallway? Running is faster!”
Explain the rule to Omar in a kind way. Think about what could happen when many students share a narrow hallway.
Give at least two reasons.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Read the story “The Night Bell.” Then retell it to a classmate who was absent.

In the village of Pine Hollow, an old bell rang every evening to call the farmers home. One winter, the bell cracked and stopped ringing. The farmers argued about who should pay for a new one, and nobody agreed.

One stormy night, a young shepherd named Anil did not come home. The farmers searched in the dark but could not find him. Then Old Ms. Pereira banged on a metal pot, and everyone joined in with pots and spoons. Anil heard the loud clanging and followed the sound back to the village.
The next morning, the farmers put their money together and bought a new bell. From then on, they agreed that everyone in Pine Hollow would help take care of it.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Leila is adding 1/2 and 1/4 for a recipe. She says: “1 + 1 = 2 and 2 + 4 = 6, so 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6.”
Picture two fraction strips of the same size. One strip is cut into 2 equal parts. The other strip is cut into 4 equal parts.
You are the math helper in the class. Tell Leila what went wrong and show her how to add the fractions.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your class is choosing a class helper for the month. The teacher says the class can pick one way to vote. Here are the two plans.
Plan A, raise your hand: The vote takes about 5 minutes. Everyone can see how everyone votes. Some students may feel shy about voting in front of friends.
Plan B, secret paper vote: Each student writes a name on a small paper and folds it. The teacher counts the papers, so the vote takes about 15 minutes. No one sees how another student voted.
Speak to your class. Choose one plan and tell why it is better.

items.stem: Read about the market scene. Then describe it in your own words so your friend can imagine it.

checklist: I described at least four things in the scene.
I used color or size words.
I said where things are (in front, behind, near, under).
I spoke in clear sentences.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: describes at least four people or objects accurately, in the learner’s own words, so a listener can imagine the scene.
Organization: moves through the scene in a logical way, such as front to back.
Vocabulary: color, size, and place words (green, tall, behind, under, near).
Sentence-level language: noun groups with adjectives (a woman in a green apron, a brown dog) and prepositional phrases.

support.clue: Look for people, things, colors, and places in the description. Start with the front and then move to the back.
support.frame: In the front of the market, I see ______. Behind ______, there is ______. Near ______, there are ______. In the background, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a classroom: “In the front of the room, I see a teacher with a purple scarf. Behind her, there is a large map. Near the window, there are two plants. On the floor, a gray rug has a book on it.” Now describe the market in the same way.

items.stem: Use the test results to choose the best material for a rain umbrella and give a reason.

checklist: I said which material I choose.
I gave a reason from the test results.
I told what happened with at least one other material.
I used because in my answer.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: chooses one material and supports the choice with evidence from the results.
Evidence: names a specific result (the cup stayed dry, or the water went through the other materials).
Sentence-level language: because or since to connect the claim and evidence; comparison with another material.
Vocabulary: words such as material, water, dry, damp, and through used accurately.

support.clue: Read each result. Which material kept the cup dry? Think about what an umbrella must do when it rains.
support.frame: I choose the ______ for the umbrella because ______. When the class tested ______, the water ______. The other materials ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a lunch bag: “I choose the metal lunch box to keep the sandwich flat because it did not bend when the class sat on it. The paper bag was squashed. The plastic bag bent a little.” Now choose a material for the umbrella.

facts: Plastic sheets do not let water pass through.
The test results in the prompt: paper towel wet, cotton damp, plastic dry.

items.stem: Tell a story about how Kofi feels and what happens next at the swimming pool.

checklist: I told how Kofi feels and why.
My story has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
I used past-tense verbs for the events.
I used at least two time words (first, then, finally).
exemplar: Task fulfilment: continues the scene with a story that includes Kofi's feeling and a beginning, middle, and end.
Organization: events are connected in time order and the ending resolves the situation.
Elaboration: includes detail about feelings, actions, or the setting (for example, Ms. Lin's hand, the cheering).
Sentence-level language: past-tense narration and time or feeling words (nervous, finally, then).
Vocabulary: feeling words and action verbs beyond basic words.

support.clue: Use the details in the scene: his toes, his arms, the teacher's hand, and the classmates. They show how he feels. Then imagine what could happen next.
support.frame: Kofi feels ______ because ______. First, ______. Then, ______. In the end, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a lost puppy: “Mei found a lost puppy in the park. She felt worried because it was shivering. First, she wrapped it in her coat. Then she read the tag on its collar. In the end, she carried the puppy home to its owner.” Now tell your story about Kofi.

items.stem: Tell the new family what they need to know about the town library.

checklist: I told when the library is open.
I told how to get a library card and what you can borrow.
I told about at least one more service.
I put similar facts together (when, what, who).
exemplar: Task fulfilment: gives at least four accurate facts from the card, including hours and the card or borrowing rule.
Organization: groups related information (hours, card and borrowing, programs and spaces).
Vocabulary: library card, borrow, computers, and story time used accurately.
Sentence-level language: present-tense statements and modal verbs (you can borrow, you need a card).
Audience awareness: speaks to the family with welcoming, clear phrasing.

support.clue: Read the card. Sort the facts into groups: when to go, how to join, what you can do there.
support.frame: The library is open ______. To get a card, ______. You can borrow ______ for ______. Children can also ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a swimming pool: “The pool is open from 10:00 to 5:00 every day except Monday. To swim, you need a pass, which costs two dollars. You can rent a towel at the desk. Children can also take lessons on Saturday mornings.” Now tell the family about the library.

items.stem: Explain to Omar why students walk, not run, in the school hallway.

checklist: I answered Omar's question kindly.
I gave two reasons for the rule.
I said what could happen if students run.
I used because, so, or if ... then.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: gives at least two reasons (for example, collisions, falls, noise, blocked doors) and answers Omar's idea that running is faster.
Cause and effect: shows the link between running and a possible result.
Sentence-level language: connectors (because, so, if ... then) and polite, kind phrasing for a younger listener.
Vocabulary: words such as hallway, crowded, bump, safe used accurately.

support.clue: Picture the hallway when many students are in it at once. What could happen if someone runs around a corner?
support.frame: We walk in the hallway because ______. If a student runs, ______. Then ______. So walking helps ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a library: “We use quiet voices in the library because other people are reading. If a student shouts, the readers cannot think. Then they feel upset. So quiet voices help everyone enjoy the library.” Now explain the hallway rule to Omar.

items.stem: Retell the story “The Night Bell” in your own words, including the problem and how it was solved.

checklist: I told the setting, the problem, and the solution.
I told the events in the right order.
I used my own words and did not read the story word for word.
I used linking words such as when, after, so, and then.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: retells the setting, the problem (the broken bell and the missing shepherd), the solution (the pots and spoons), and the ending.
Organization: clear beginning, middle, and end with events in order.
Sentence-level language: past-tense narration with connectors that show time and cause (when, after, so, because).
Elaboration: includes why the problem mattered (the farmers could not find Anil) and what changed at the end.
Clarity: uses paraphrase rather than reading, with names used correctly.

support.clue: Find the problem, what the farmers tried, and what finally worked. Then find what the farmers did at the end.
support.frame: In the story, ______. The problem was ______. First, ______. Then ______. Finally, ______. At the end, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a different story: “In the story ‘The Silver Kettle,’ a family lives on a mountain. The problem was that their well dried up. First, the father walked to a faraway river. Then the children dug a channel from the river to the garden. Finally, the water reached the garden. At the end, the family shared the water with their neighbors.” Now retell “The Night Bell.”

items.stem: Explain to Leila why 2/6 is not the answer, and show her step by step how to add 1/2 and 1/4.

checklist: I said that 2/6 is not correct and gave a reason.
I explained that halves and fourths are different-sized pieces.
I changed 1/2 into fourths before adding.
I used the words first, then, and so to show my steps.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states that 2/6 is wrong and gives the correct sum, 3/4.
Mathematical reasoning: shows that 1/2 = 2/4, then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4; may also notice that 2/6 is less than 1/2, so it cannot be the sum of 1/2 and another amount.
Vocabulary: fraction, equal parts, halves, fourths, and equal to or equivalent used accurately.
Sentence-level language: step words (first, then, so) and reasons with because or if ... then.
Clarity: keeps each fraction in view so the listener can follow each step.

support.clue: Think about the size of the pieces. Are halves and fourths the same size? How could you cut the half so its pieces match the fourths? Also ask: should the total be more than 1/2 or less?
support.frame: Leila added the ______ and the ______, but the pieces are ______ sizes. First, I change 1/2 into ______. Now both fractions have ______. Then ______ + ______ = ______. So 1/2 + 1/4 = ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About lengths: “Dev says 30 cm + 2 m = 32. I disagree with Dev. The units are different, so I cannot add the numbers yet. First, I change 2 m into 200 cm. Now both lengths are in centimeters. Then 30 + 200 = 230. So the total is 230 cm.” Now help Leila with her fractions.

facts: 2/6 = 1/3, which is less than 1/2, so 2/6 cannot be the sum of 1/2 and another positive amount.
Adding the numerators and the denominators separately is not a correct way to add fractions.

items.stem: Choose raise-your-hand voting or a secret paper vote for your class and justify your choice, including one drawback of your plan.

checklist: I clearly chose Plan A or Plan B.
I gave two reasons that use details from the plans.
I named one drawback of my plan and answered it.
I used although or however.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: chooses one plan, gives at least two reasons based on the plan details, and addresses a drawback.
Evidence: uses specific details (5 minutes, 15 minutes, everyone can see, feel shy, no one sees how another student voted).
Organization: claim, reasons, drawback with response, and a closing sentence.
Sentence-level language: complex sentences with although, however, or even though; a respectful tone for classmates.
Elaboration: explains why a detail matters to the class (for example, fairness, feeling safe to choose, or time for learning).

support.clue: Make a list of what is good and what is hard about each plan. Choose the plan you can defend best, and plan what to say about its weak point.
support.frame: I believe the town should choose Plan ______ because ______. Also, ______. Although ______, ______. That is why Plan ______ is better.
support.model: Mentor example. About a family trip: “I believe our family should take the train because we can look out the window. Also, nobody has to drive, so everyone can relax. Although the train is slower than the car, we can read and play cards. That is why the train is better.” Now make your choice for the class vote.
